Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Navy Officer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crowding: Crowded places, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others

Vignette:
Three years ago, during a sudden hurricane strike that breached the eastern seaboard, Lieutenant Elias Vance was stationed in the lower engineering sector of a coastal naval facility. The storm surge poured through the seawalls in minutes, flooding wide corridors into fast-moving currents. Elias found himself wedged against a rusted bulkhead in a narrow stairwell, his knees drawn up and shoulders hunched, as dozens of personnel scrambled past him in a crushing wave of bodies. Emergency response teams doused the area with alcohol-based fire retardants to prevent electrical shorts, and the sharp, chemical sting of high-proof alcohol filled the choking air. For forty minutes, the space was pitch black, the only illumination coming from fractured overhead panels. He watched the water rise in sharp, disconnected frames—shattered safety glass, a drifting clipboard, the grim faces of men fighting the current—and felt his own body locked in the exact posture he had held on the metal stairs. When the water finally receded, he told himself the whole ordeal felt like something that had happened to someone else, a sequence of images too extreme to be his own reality. In the months that followed, certain physical locations on base, particularly the lower stairwells and the flooded corridor he had navigated, made his chest tighten before he even stepped inside. He began taking the long upper routes, even when it meant missing briefings, because the lower levels carried the same oppressive geometry. Crowding became another source of quiet dread. During a base-wide muster, he backed out of the assembly hall when the perimeter filled, his breath catching as the mass of people pressing in triggered the exact sensation of being pinned against the bulkhead. Then there was the smell. A supply sergeant sprayed industrial alcohol-based cleaner in the hallway, and the vapor hit him like a physical weight. He left his station immediately, pacing the outdoor tarmac until his heart slowed, certain that the scent meant another breach, another flood, another night trapped in the dark. Parallel to these reactions, his perspective on himself and his world shifted. He had come to believe he used to be a happy person, the kind who laughed easily and looked forward to weekends, but now he felt a constant, grinding misery that followed him home. His wife, Sarah, asked why he kept retreating to the guest room or declining invitations, and he could only shrug. He had started avoiding his old Navy friends, telling himself they would not understand, and when they did reach out, he stayed silent. The distance between him and his former life deepened into a conviction that he no longer belonged anywhere. He stopped attending unit gatherings, canceled sports, and kept to the periphery of his own marriage. He told himself he deserved to suffer because of what had happened, as if enduring his own withdrawal was a quiet penance for surviving. He also began avoiding the lower maintenance bays and storage corridors where the overhead lights burned out, because the dark pressed against him with the same weight as the flooded corridor. Now, at thirty-four, Elias serves as a logistics officer aboard a naval vessel, a role that requires navigating tight bulkheads and crowded mess decks daily. The contrast between his current posting and his past dread has become unsustainable. During a recent fire drill, he stood frozen in a dimly lit passageway, his shoulders hunching instinctively, the darkness pressing against him like the breached lower deck. He realized he could no longer outrun the images, the bodily tension, or the certainty that he had drifted entirely out of reach of the life he once knew. What finally brought him to a mental health clinic was not a single breaking point, but the accumulating weight of waking up exhausted, declining every social invitation, and feeling completely set apart from his own years. He hopes to understand why his body still keeps returning to that stairwell, and what he might do to stop believing he deserves to carry it alone.
